The First Brands/Apollo episode (O4ayidFGsGM) is ~80% an operations interview (Don Kieffer, MIT Sloan, There's Got to Be a Better Way); the EA episode and the First Brands bankruptcy episode spend half their time on Fed funds vs SOFR, gold, and a naked-short Treasury trader. ⚠ Bias. The hosts are ex-sell-side and came up in the 2007 CLO and rates world. Kristen defends CLOs hard, and her own data point for that defense ("defaults were like 2%", repeated in two episodes) is wrong (see §18). Guests are often selling an asset class. Findley is raising a fund and quotes her own returns. Gatto runs Silver Point's private credit and is "100%" sure private credit is good for society, while plugging his book throughout. Gornick's current job is selling Churchill's funds to the wealth channel, and her "remarkably low loss rates" claim predates a real cycle. Kroboth jokes about fundraising and frames his smaller AUM as discipline. Two bond shorts are paid ads for Public.com's bond account. The Global Alts host runs the conference whose meeting counts he quotes. Indap and Carissa Jordan (no longer at a bank) are the most neutral voices. Several figures are misspoken on air ("$30 million" for the $30bn Caesars LBO, "$6 million" for First Brands' $6bn refinancing, VICI as a "$50 million company", the Gatto episode "filmed in November of 2020" when First Brands and Tricolor date it to late 2025). Each is flagged where it appears. The hosts also cite ChatGPT and Claude as sources for BDC leverage and Affinity's AUM, so treat those numbers as unverified.

What this adds to the program

  • The lender's side of every deal. The repo teaches the LBO from the equity seat (tiger sisters private capital 101: house analogy, Toys R Us) and leverage as a balance-sheet ratio (learn/unit-04-is-it-healthy.md). Nothing here covers how debt is priced, layered, documented, traded, or taken away. This note adds credit spreads, seniority and structural subordination, covenants, recovery rates, and the playbook equity uses against debt.
  • Agency cost of debt, made concrete. canon jensen meckling agency theory covers managers versus shareholders. The 1976 paper's other half, where equity expropriates creditors once leverage is high, is missing from the repo. Caesars is that half acted out in full: asset transfers to an affiliate, guarantee stripping, conflicted fairness opinions.
  • Private credit as a structure, not a buzzword. Direct lending as it is actually built (middle-market tiers, unitranche, delayed-draw loans, the 150–250bp premium and what it buys), asset-based lending, the three kinds of semi-liquid retail vehicle and why each gates differently, insurer balance sheets, and why the 2026 stress looks like "2008 with the leverage moved". None of it is in the repo.
  • The plumbing of a bond. How a bond is born (syndicate, book, Treasury plus spread) and how it then trades (OTC dealers, spread vs price quoting, agency trading, portfolio trades, CDS indices). The repo's trading floor mechanics covers the floor; this adds the credit product itself.
  • Why the bottom of a capital structure is a negotiation, not a formula. Distressed strategies (pull to par, distress for control, capital-structure relative value), valuation fights, liability management exercises with a worked uptier, capital-solutions lending, CDS as a weapon as well as a hedge, and the reason a 2026 first-lien loan recovers about 60 cents where it once recovered about 80.
  • A direct challenge to the accounting core. Course 01 material (summaries/core-01-accounting.json) teaches the current ratio as a liquidity measure. Gatto, who teaches credit at Columbia and Fordham, calls it analytically useless. §5 sets out why a lender looks elsewhere.
  • A judgment hook for acumen/. Every concept below gives a falsifiable question to ask of a live credit: who controls the documents, who can be layered, and who is forced to sell.

1 · Credit asymmetry & expected loss

What it is. A lender's best case is fixed: collect the coupons and get the face value ("par") back. The worst case is losing most of the principal. So credit investing is about avoiding the bad outcome rather than finding the great one. The hosts' version: equity has to pick winners, credit just has to avoid losers. Gatto's version is about temperament. A venture investor can take zeros on six deals out of ten as long as it doesn't miss the next Facebook; a lender's job is to never make the mistake, so the credit analyst is professionally glass-half-empty.

How it works. Any pool of loans comes down to two assumptions: what share defaults, and how much you recover on the ones that do. Expected loss = default rate × (1 − recovery rate). The channel's stress case (Kristen recalling a Blackstone executive, Private Credit: The Best Explanation): even at a 15% cumulative default rate and 50% recovery, the book loses 15% × 0.5 = 7.5% of principal. Painful, and it ends the 10–12% return story, but it is nowhere near the 100-to-zero of an equity wipeout. Annualized illustration (not from the channel): 3% default × (1 − 0.70) = 0.9% a year of loss, which a 10% coupon easily covers; at 8% defaults and 60% recovery the loss is 3.2% a year, and the coupon carries a levered fund only if nothing else goes wrong. Anchor recoveries on air: CLO models assumed about 70 cents on senior loans (Kristen, in three episodes). In the financial crisis you expected about 70 on senior debt and about 40 on bonds (Caesars Pt 2). Moody's now shows first-lien recoveries near 60 cents, down from about 80 (Indap, Pt 3).

Business significance / value. This is why lenders charge a spread, demand collateral and write covenants: every tool exists to push recovery up or default down. It is also why credit funds lever up. A 10% asset with a capped upside only reaches equity-like returns if you borrow against it (§12). Gatto says every Silver Point credit memo now carries a section on AI vulnerability: a borrower that covers its coupon easily today may not in four years, and the analyst who says "we're not worried about that" is the one he expects to blow up.

Forces & impact. Recoveries depend on what sits below you in the structure (§6), on how much leverage the deal carries, on what is left to sell (a pipe-fittings maker leaves more residual value than a SaaS wrapper, Jen's point in the 2008 deep dive), and on whether other creditors can jump ahead of you (§14). All of these have moved against lenders since 2015, and that is the core of the "it's worse than 2008" argument.

With vs. without. Without the asymmetry framing, investors read a 10–11% yield on "senior secured" loans as low risk and high reward, which is how BCRED was sold (shorts, lAF2ujd64GU). With it, you ask what the yield pays you for, and the answer is default and recovery risk plus illiquidity.

Applies when / Breaks when. Applies to every performing loan. Breaks when the instrument has hidden upside, as in distressed debt bought at 10–40 cents (§15), where returns look like equity. Findley's re-REMIC mezzanine bonds bought at about 10 cents are the extreme case.

Channel example. The BEST EXPLAINER you'll get on Private Credit Funds like Blackstone's BCRED or Blue Owl's OBDC (short). The 15/50 stress case from Private Credit: The Best Explanation of Exactly What's Happening. Gatto's memo discipline from Distressed Debt 101 with the GOAT. Recovery data from Financial Times Reporter TELLS ALL: Why Private Credit is Worse than Credit in 2008.

Counterpoint. The short's "low risk, high reward" framing of BCRED is a straw man. Nobody serious priced it that way, since the yield was mostly SOFR plus an illiquidity premium during a high-rate period. The 15/50 stress case comes secondhand from a manager defending its own fund, and it ignores fund leverage: a 7.5% principal loss on a book levered 1:1 is roughly 15% of investor equity. The 70/40 GFC recovery numbers are roughly right for loans and bonds respectively, though dated: they predate cov-lite and loan-only structures.

Links. canon klarman margin of safety (lender's margin of safety = recovery cushion), canon taleb black swan (capped upside, fat left tail), canon grove only the paranoid survive (Gatto's credit temperament).

2 · Credit spreads

What it is. A company's borrowing rate has two parts: a base rate (Treasury yield or SOFR) that everyone pays, and a credit spread that pays the lender for this borrower's default risk. Spreads are quoted in basis points (bp; 100bp = 1%).

How it works. The tariff short's arithmetic: Treasuries at 4% plus a 150bp spread gives a 5.5% all-in cost. When tariffs hit, the base rate fell (money fled into Treasuries) but spreads widened, because default risk rose through three channels: higher input costs, weaker demand at higher prices, and retaliation abroad. So the US government's borrowing got cheaper while leveraged companies' borrowing got dearer. The Oracle episode shows the market-level gauge: CDX IG, the index of CDS on investment-grade names, widened to roughly 40bp while Oracle's own spread widened by about 95bp. The investor's side of the same arithmetic (a sponsored corporate-bond short): a 5% five-year Treasury plus a 170bp spread locks in 6.7%. If Treasuries don't move but the spread tightens to 150bp, new bonds yield 6.5% and the 6.7% bond rises in price. A bondholder earns from falling rates or tightening spreads, and loses on either moving the other way.

Business significance / value. The spread is the price of access to capital. It decides whether a maturity can be refinanced (First Brands could not), whether an LBO pencils out, and whether a hyperscaler can keep funding capex with debt. Indap's note on the record investment-grade week (Amazon, Honeywell) shows the other side: treasurers rush to issue when spreads are tight and windows open.

Forces & impact. Spreads compress when investors hunt for yield. Jen's "cash trap" argument: front-end investors pre-buy Fed cuts, then stretch further out the curve and down the credit spectrum, and spreads reach all-time tights. Credit Trading 101 gives the mechanism. With Treasury yields high, "yield-based buyers" buy corporate bonds outright for the all-in yield instead of hedging out the rate component, so their demand lands on the spread. On air, IG spreads were at their tightest since 2007 while default rates sat around a historically normal 3% (Carissa, citing a Barclays credit strategist). Spreads widen on defaults, fraud headlines and recession signals. Second-order effect: tight spreads loosen terms (cov-lite, PIK toggles), and loose terms make the next widening worse.

With vs. without. If spreads did not move with risk, risky borrowers would fund at the government's rate and lenders would be paid nothing for default, which was roughly the 2006–07 condition. When spreads stay tight for too long, everyone short credit is "dying" (Jen on First Brands): the negative carry of being right too early kills the position before the event arrives.

Applies when / Breaks when. Applies to traded credit. It breaks in private credit, where a loan "identifies as par" (Jen) because it is marked to model, not to market. Spread widening shows up late there, as markdowns and dividend cuts (§12).

Channel example. Tariff Fallout: Why Are Credit Spreads Widening? (short). Oracle CDS: the "Anti-AI Trade". Why Apollo Was Blacklisted By First Brands, where First Brands broke and spreads "didn't budge". Credit Trading 101 (tights with 3% defaults). How does investing in corporate bonds work? (short, a Public.com ad).

Counterpoint. The tariff short treats spreads as a pure function of fundamentals. In practice technical demand matters as much: insurer and retail inflows can hold spreads tight through real deterioration, which is the hosts' own point elsewhere and the Barclays strategist's whole argument. Jen's cash-trap thesis is her hypothesis, not consensus. The corporate-bond short is an ad promising to "lock in" 6.7%; that yield is locked only if you hold to maturity and nothing defaults, and a blend of IG and high yield at 170bp is a portfolio average, not a risk level.

Links. bloomberg terminal instrumentation (CDS, WB spread screens the program cannot reproduce for free), trading floor mechanics.

3 · Where bonds come from: DCM, syndicates & ratings

What it is. A bond is a tradable slice of a loan. The debt capital markets (DCM) group sits between investment banking and sales & trading: it helps a company decide what debt to issue, then a syndicate of banks underwrites it (commits to buy the whole issue if investors don't) and sells it on to investors. Investment-grade issuers are covered by DCM proper; high-yield issuers, often LBO companies, by leveraged finance (levfin).

How it works. The hosts' worked example (DCM 101): Amazon borrowing about $13.7bn to buy Whole Foods, with Goldman, Bank of America and JPMorgan as the syndicate and maturities out to 40 years. 1. Underwriting spread. If the syndicate commits at 98 and sells to investors at 100, the 2 points are its fee and its cushion against the market moving before the bonds are placed. 2. Pricing = risk-free + spread. Take the on-the-run Treasury of the same tenor (say 5% for 10 years), add the issuer's credit spread (say 100bp for Amazon), and the coupon is 6%. Longer tenor costs more (the hosts' 6% for 10 years vs 8% for 40), and weaker credit costs more. 3. Building the book. Fixed-income salespeople collect orders from Fidelity, BlackRock, Vanguard and the like. A hot book (the hosts' hypothetical: $45bn of orders for $13.7bn of bonds) lets the syndicate tighten "price talk", so the issuer pays a lower yield. In 2026, Amazon's record issuance day was about 3.5x oversubscribed (Jen, Private Credit Deep Dive), and she warns books are padded. 4. Pricing call and allocation. On pricing day a trader calls the Treasury level, the spread is added, and the bond is born. The lead underwriter decides allocations; per Carissa, its traders weigh in on who is "real money" and who will flip. The bond then "breaks" and the trader sends the first two-way market, sometimes minutes after allocation.

Ratings set the boundary. S&P, Moody's and Fitch run AAA, AA, A, BBB (investment grade, down to BBB−), then BB, B, CCC (high yield, BB+ and below), then default. High-yield issues need size to trade: Kristen's rule of thumb was at least about $200M, and the smallest issue Carissa ever traded was about $150M, which "you never see again" once placed.

Business significance / value. DCM turns a company's need for long-term money into securities that thousands of investors can hold in small pieces, so no single bank has to carry Amazon for 40 years. The bank earns the underwriting spread and the relationship. The issuer gets price discovery; the investor gets a liquid claim.

Forces & impact. Issuance windows open and shut with rates and sentiment, which is why treasurers rush to issue when spreads are tight (Amazon and Honeywell in 2026). Ratings are partly backward-looking: Carissa notes that in 2008 many companies trading like junk were still rated investment grade. The US itself lost its AAA, and on air only Microsoft and Johnson & Johnson (plus Apple at one agency) are named as AAA corporates. Second-order: the BBB−/BB+ line drives forced selling when a "fallen angel" is downgraded, because many IG mandates cannot hold high yield.

With vs. without. Without an underwritten syndicate, every large borrower would have to find its own lenders, and market moves during the sale would land on the issuer. With it, the bank absorbs that risk, which is exactly what goes wrong in a "hung" deal such as the Twitter buyout debt banks were stuck with in 2022–23 (Gatto).

Applies when / Breaks when. Works for rated issuers in open markets. Breaks for small or complex borrowers that can't be rated or syndicated, which is the opening for direct lending (§8), and when markets shut between commitment and sale. Gornick's point: a bank can give price talk, but on pricing day the terms can "flex" wider or the deal can die.

Channel example. 5. Debt Capital Markets 101: Where Do Bonds Come From?. Credit Trading 101 (syndicate desk and allocation). Private Credit Deep Dive (Amazon's 2026 deal).

Counterpoint. The Amazon walkthrough is simplified to the point of error. Amazon's 2017 Whole Foods financing was a $16bn multi-tranche bond, not $13.7bn, and a 2-point underwriting spread is a high-yield number; investment-grade gross spreads run well under 1% of face. Kristen's mortgage aside says the 10-year "went down 3.25%" in a day; a move of that size never happened, and she probably means basis points or a yield level. The hosts admit the episode is outside their seat ("go easy on us").

Links. wss capital markets ma (§2, the equity bookbuild, same syndicate mechanics), trading floor mechanics (where the syndicate desk sits).

4 · How credit trades: dealers, quotes and the shrinking risk book

What it is. After issuance, corporate bonds trade over the counter (OTC): no exchange, just investors asking dealers (Goldman, JPMorgan, BofA) for a two-way price. "Credit" in trading means corporate bonds and corporate CDS, split into leveraged loans, investment grade, high yield and distressed, with converts and preferreds as hybrids (Credit Trading 101).

How it works. Carissa's mechanics: - Quoting. IG trades as a spread over Treasuries in basis points; HY and distressed trade in dollar price (99 bid, 99.5 offered). Because price and yield move inversely, an IG dealer's bid spread is the higher number. Distressed paper is quoted in price because a 40,000bp spread means nothing; "call it 60" does. - Size. Standard markets are about $5M in IG and about $2M in HY. A standard Treasury ticket is about $100M, so credit is a much thinner market. - Hedging. An IG buyer usually sells Treasuries against the bond, weighted by DV01 (the dollar change per 1bp move), to isolate the spread. If the client doesn't, the dealer hedges through its rates desk. - Agency vs risk. Dealers once bought bonds into inventory and worked out of them. Since Volcker they mostly match a buyer and seller at the same time. HY bid-ask is about half a point, but a matched agency trade may earn only 1/8 or 1/16. - Portfolio trading. Instead of bid-wanted lists (BWICs) priced bond by bond, managers send a whole portfolio for one price, built off third-party pricing. Portfolio trades are about 10% of TRACE volume (TRACE is the public tape of bond trades). - Desks. Distressed has its own desk, staffed with lawyers reading documents, and is dominated by hedge funds; real money appears when it has to work out of a position.

Business significance / value. Market-making is what makes a bond worth more than a loan: you can sell it. Dealers earn the bid-ask; investors pay it as the cost of exit. For issuers, secondary prices set the level of the next deal, so traders and syndicate desks constantly compare notes on where existing bonds trade and who holds them.

Forces & impact. Post-crisis capital rules and Volcker shrank dealer balance sheets. Banks that once let a trader be long or short $50M of one bond now balk, desks are staffed by "junior risk takers" who never traded through 2008, and the job shifted to agency matching. Electronic and algorithmic trading make IG "more equity-like". Second-order: liquidity is now conditional. In calm markets it's cheap; in stress, nobody warehouses risk, so prices gap. Funding costs matter again with rates high: a dealer long a bond is borrowing to hold it.

With vs. without. Without dealers willing to hold inventory, bonds behave more like private loans, easy to buy and hard to sell. With agency-only dealers, the buyer of last resort is missing exactly when needed, which is the opening distressed and capital-solutions funds fill (§15, §16).

Applies when / Breaks when. The two-way market works for large, liquid issues and index names. It breaks for small issues ($150M), off-index names, and anything in distress, where the trade happens only at a price someone with a legal edge will pay.

Channel example. Credit Trading 101 (Carissa Jordan, ex-Goldman, started on the IG desk in July 2008).

Counterpoint. Jen calls TRACE a post-crisis requirement; TRACE actually launched in 2002, and post-crisis rules expanded it and shortened reporting lags. The "tightest since 2007 with 3% defaults" data point was true when recorded but is a snapshot. Carissa is candid that she left trading years ago and some current-practice figures are secondhand.

Links. trading floor mechanics (desk roles, sales vs trading), wss trading hedge funds (fast money, basis trades), bloomberg terminal instrumentation (ALLQ-style dealer quotes the program cannot see for free).

5 · Leverage, coverage, covenants & liquidity

What it is. Leverage = debt / EBITDA (EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, a rough proxy for operating cash flow). It roughly says how many years of current cash flow it would take to repay the debt. Coverage = EBITDA / interest: how many times over the company can pay a year's interest. Covenants are contract terms that trip when these ratios cross a line.

How it works. The tariff short's example: $400M debt / $100M EBITDA = 4.0x against a 6.0x covenant, so the company is fine. EBITDA falls to $50M and leverage becomes 8.0x, a breach without borrowing a dollar more. Caesars: $24bn / $3bn = 8x at inception, coverage 1.5x. By 2014 EBITDA was about $1.5bn, $300M below OpCo interest alone. OpCo leverage reached 14–16x and then 18x, coverage about 0.5x, free cash flow about −$1bn a year. Kristen's conservative variant is (EBITDA − capex) / interest, because capex is real cash. Two covenant styles: maintenance covenants are tested every quarter; incurrence covenants are tested only when the company acts (borrows more, pays a dividend). Cov-lite loans carry only incurrence tests.

Who gets which: in the middle market, direct lenders insist on quarterly financial maintenance covenants that the syndicated market dropped (Gornick, counterintuitively: the borrower pays a premium and accepts tighter terms), though in the competitive upper middle market some direct deals now carry none. Kroboth's non-negotiables as a special-situations lender are a covenant, downside protection, and limits on EBITDA add-backs (the "adjustments" that inflate the EBITDA the ratios are tested on).

Liquidity, not the current ratio. Gatto's book calls the current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities), standard in accounting courses, analytically meaningless as a liquidity measure; Jen reads the passage on air. His reasons and his multi-step replacement are left as a spoiler. The usual lender objections (not from the channel): inventory and receivables are not cash, and the ratio ignores revolver availability, cash burn and debt maturities. A working version: cash plus undrawn committed revolver, less minimum operating cash, set against the next 12–24 months of burn, interest and maturities.

Business significance / value. Covenants are the lender's early-warning system and seat at the table. A breach forces a negotiation while value still exists, and that is the whole point. Caesars had effectively one covenant that mattered (senior secured debt/EBITDA), breached in 2014.

Forces & impact. Competition among lenders trades covenants away for yield. Kristen ties the shift from maintenance to incurrence covenants directly to investors reaching for spread. Gatto sorts current deals into good, fine and bad (bad meaning the lender is not paid for the risk). In a normal market the bad ones fail to raise money; he now sees all three getting done, his marker of the overheated phase of the cycle. The second-order effect: without tripwires, the first sign of trouble is a missed payment or a fraud discovery, by which point recoveries have already fallen.

With vs. without. With maintenance covenants, Caesars' lenders would have had leverage over Apollo years before the asset transfers. Without them (and with the $4.5bn of old Harrah's bonds that carried no change-of-control protection), lenders learned their position was being reshaped only after the fact.

Applies when / Breaks when. EBITDA-based ratios apply to steady cash-flow businesses. They break for asset-light software where "adjusted EBITDA" is negotiable, and wherever EBITDA itself is fraudulent (First Brands).

Channel example. Tariff Fallout (short). Private Equity's Blueprint For Legally Stealing From its Creditors | Caesars LBO (Pt 1/3). Distressed Debt 102 (Pt 2/3). What is Private Credit? | Direct Lending Explained (maintenance covenants). Distressed Debt 101 with the GOAT (current ratio, deal tiers). Private Credit: The Best Explanation (Kroboth's non-negotiables).

Counterpoint. Kristen says a post-2008 rule capped LBOs at 6x and attributes it to "when Obama came in" or "the SEC". It was the 2013 interagency leveraged-lending guidance (Fed, OCC, FDIC), which applied to banks, not to private lenders, and was softened in 2018. That is precisely why the risk migrated to non-banks. The "years to repay" reading of leverage ignores interest and capex, so it overstates repayment capacity. Gatto's "the current ratio is a joke" is deliberately provocative; the ratio is crude rather than useless for a trade creditor screening thousands of small accounts.

Links. learn/unit-04-is-it-healthy.md (balance-sheet leverage), canon jensen meckling agency theory (covenants as bonding devices).

6 · Capital structure, security & structural subordination

What it is. The capital structure ranks claims: senior secured loans, then junior/second-lien debt, then unsecured bonds, then equity. Senior means first in line; secured means a claim on specific assets or cash flows (Jen: security need not be a building; it can be the business's cash flows). Structural subordination means a lender to a parent ranks behind lenders to the subsidiary that actually owns the assets, because it is "further from the cash". Equity at the bottom is, in her words, a hope that something is left.

How it works. Jen's image is a cereal dispenser: losses empty from the bottom up. Every bond is a contract, and its indenture sets which entities guarantee it and what it is secured by (Gatto), which is why two bonds of the same company can be worth very different amounts in default (§15). Caesars added a legal-entity layer: a parent over an OpCo (runs the casinos) and a PropCo (owns the buildings, leased back to the OpCo). The PropCo carried $6.5bn of CMBS, mortgage debt the OpCo lenders could not touch. Kristen's Kim Kardashian analogy: a lender to the Skims business cannot foreclose on the Calabasas house, because the mortgage lender holds it. The OpCo debt was guaranteed by the parent, which gave OpCo creditors a claim on parent value. Apollo later attacked exactly that link (§14). Special-purpose vehicles (SPVs) are the hidden version. Gatto: a company that pledges receivables and inventory for a $100M revolver shows $100M of debt. Move those assets into a separate legal entity, structure the borrowing so the accountants allow both assets and debt off the balance sheet, and the same economic loan disappears from view. How much debt sat in SPVs was his headline First Brands red flag, and it was Enron's.

Business significance / value. OpCo/PropCo splits let a sponsor borrow cheaply against real estate (subsidized mortgage markets, a REIT's tax advantage) on top of cash-flow debt. Caesars got about two extra turns of leverage this way. The PropCo later emerged from bankruptcy as VICI, a REIT that Caesars pays more than $1bn a year in rent (Indap).

Forces & impact. Every new entity is a seam where value can be moved. Indap adds a modern point: lease payments to VICI are "effectively debt", so Caesars' roughly $15bn of debt understates its real fixed claims. The same applies to any sale-leaseback.

With vs. without. A single-entity borrower gives all lenders one pool to fight over. Multi-entity structures give the equity sponsor a map of where to relocate assets. That map is the precondition for drop-downs.

Applies when / Breaks when. Seniority holds in a clean bankruptcy. It breaks when documents permit priming, layering or entity transfers (§14), when a court values the company low enough to wipe a class out (§15), and when lease and off-balance-sheet obligations (First Brands' $10–11bn included off-balance-sheet financing) are counted as something other than debt. Project-finance SPVs (Meta's Hyperion data center, §18) are the legitimate use: lenders deliberately sit closer to one asset's cash flows.

Channel example. Caesars LBO (Pt 1/3). Indap on VICI and the lease-as-debt point in Pt 3. Private Equity vs. Private Credit Explained in less than 90 seconds (short). Gatto on SPVs in Distressed Debt 101.

Counterpoint. The hosts report VICI as a "$50 million" company. They mean billions, and even then the figure is closer to enterprise value than market cap. Kristen also says lenders "typically" take ownership in a bankruptcy. That is true for the fulcrum class only, not senior lenders who are paid in full. Gatto says SPVs are designed "for the most part" to hide debt; securitization SPVs also exist to isolate assets and lower funding costs, and most are disclosed in footnotes, which is his real point: read them.

Links. tiger sisters private capital 101 (equity view of the same stack), acumen/case-03-carvana.md (ABS subordinate tranches, the securitization version of the same logic).

7 · Public vs private credit: syndicated loans, HY bonds, bridges, CLOs, direct lending

What it is. Public credit is debt with a CUSIP (a tradable identifier) and a visible price. Findley: if it is CUSIP'd it's public, otherwise it's private. Private credit is a privately negotiated loan between a borrower (usually a small or mid-size private company) and a capital provider (an insurer, an alternative manager's fund, or a BDC) with no intermediary in between (Gornick). It is a catch-all: direct lending, opportunistic and special-situations credit, mezzanine, infrastructure, real estate and venture debt, and asset-based finance all qualify, with very different risk. And it is old: insurers were making private placements to mid-size companies in the 1980s. Traditionally a bank arranged a syndicated loan and parcelled it out to other banks and to CLOs (collateralized loan obligations, vehicles that pool about 200 leveraged loans and sell tranches against them). Big deals added high-yield (junk) bonds for issues above roughly $200–250M, with a bridge loan from the banks covering the gap until the bonds sold. Direct lending replaces all of that with one lender, or a small club, that originates and holds the loan.

How it works. Gatto lays out the three ways Silver Point earns from loans. In the broadly syndicated loan (BSL) market a bank finds, structures and sells the deal and you buy a small piece, mostly through CLOs, which buy 60–70% of every BSL. In private credit you do all of it yourself, take an upfront fee and coupons, and need to write $200–500M checks, because the borrower's reason for coming to you is not dealing with a hundred lenders (about $16–17bn of Silver Point's $41bn). And distressed (§15). The borrower's trade-off (Jen's short): direct lenders close in days rather than weeks, and if things go wrong you renegotiate with one counterparty instead of thousands of bondholders. In exchange you pay more: Gornick puts the premium at 150–250bp, narrowing to about 500bp versus 325–350bp in the upper middle market (§8). Loans float at SOFR (formerly LIBOR) plus a spread; HY bonds are usually fixed. The CLO warehouse: banks fund the purchase of loans for a CLO manager before the CLO prices, earning a markup and fees, and are stuck with the "parts" if buyers vanish (Jen's car-factory analogy). That happened in 2007–08. EA, 2025: JPMorgan alone committed the $20bn debt package ($18bn funded at close), the largest single-bank buyout underwrite on record. It can syndicate, issue bonds, or hold the loan on a roughly $50bn direct-lending balance sheet. In 2007 TXU's $24bn of senior loans came from a dozen banks, plus $11bn of HY via bridges.

Business significance / value. Value migrated from bank underwriting fees to asset managers' spread income. Indap's point is that the labels are dissolving: Apollo-type funds buy and hold billions of "public" deal debt, which is private credit by behaviour. Banks have come back in through direct-lending arms and by lending to private credit funds.

Forces & impact. Post-2008 capital rules and leveraged-lending guidance pushed risk out of banks. Jen in the 2008 deep dive: the risk-taking moved to what was called shadow banking, which "got a facelift" and was rebranded private credit. Zero rates and then high floating rates made private loans attractive to insurers and retail. The second-order effect is concentration. Syndication spreads one borrower across many balance sheets; a single direct lender (or JPM on EA) holds a concentrated position. Jen: securitization exists to reduce bank risk, and holding is the opposite.

With vs. without. Without the syndicated or CLO machine, banks could make each loan only once (Jen: securitization is "where bonds come from"). Without direct lending, the 2023 freeze, when banks were hung on the Twitter buyout debt and SVB failed, would have cut off credit entirely. Gatto calls private credit the lender that steps in when banks step back.

Applies when / Breaks when. Direct lending wins in mid-market deals (too small for HY) and in speed- or confidentiality-sensitive situations. It breaks when one-lender opacity hides stress (Jen: the market is designed to obscure trouble) and when too much capital chases too few deals, compressing spreads and diligence.

Channel example. Eerie Similarities Between Record Setting 2025 LBO (EA) and 2007 TXU LBO. The best explanation of why everyone is worried about Private Credit (short). Distressed Debt 101 with the GOAT and its short Is Private Credit about to Blow Up the Economy? Michael Gatto's Honest Take. What is Private Credit? | Direct Lending Explained. Private Credit Deep Dive: Is this 2008 all over again?.

Counterpoint. Gatto's case, that private credit is countercyclical and uses moderate 60% LTV with 1:1 to 2:1 fund leverage, comes from the head of a private credit business. LTV is computed on sponsor valuations at 20x EBITDA, so 60% LTV can still mean 7x+ leverage. Kristen guesses JPM won't hold all $20bn, but nobody on the episode knows the structure. In the 2008 deep dive Kristen cites Gornick as saying direct lending costs "around 100 basis points" more; Gornick's own figure was 150–250bp.

Links. trading floor mechanics (who on the floor syndicates and distributes).

8 · Direct lending mechanics: unitranche, revolvers, delayed draws and the life of a loan

What it is. How a direct loan to a private-equity-owned company is actually built. A unitranche is a single loan, one credit agreement and one blended price, that replaces a senior loan plus a junior loan from different lenders. Around it sit a revolver (a credit line the borrower draws and repays) and often a delayed-draw term loan (DDTL), committed now and drawn later.

How it works. Gornick (Churchill, Direct Lending Explained): - Market tiers by EBITDA: lower middle market below about $15M (some say $10M), core $15–75M (or $10–100M), upper middle market above about $75–100M. Borrowers in each tier look alike, so structure follows size. The big managers' books skew larger: on air, typical BCRED-type borrowers had about $250M of EBITDA (Kristen). - Classic core structure: senior debt to about 4x EBITDA, junior debt another 1–2x, so 5–5.5x total, and the rest of the price is sponsor equity. That is a three-party negotiation. - Unitranche: one lender goes from dollar one to about 5.5–7x at a blended price, so the deal is two-party (lender and sponsor). It emerged around 2018–19 and became mainstream in the 2021 boom. The edge is speed in auctions with 20–50 sponsors bidding: a committed one-lender package lets a sponsor pre-empt. "Stretch senior" sits in between. - Revolver: hard for non-banks, which have no deposits to fund a draw within 24 hours, so lenders must reserve liquidity for it. - DDTL: committed for 18–24 months for bolt-on acquisitions in buy-and-build strategies; the sponsor pays a ticking fee on the unused amount and loses it if not drawn. - Terms: 5–7 year maturity, about 1% a year amortization, a small call premium early (101–102) and freely prepayable after. Loans are usually refinanced or repaid around year 3–4, mostly on a sale, and about 20% of the portfolio repays each year, so origination has to keep running just to stay invested. A "portable" loan that follows the company to a new owner is rare and very borrower-friendly. - Price: the premium over syndicated debt is 150–250bp. Gornick's arithmetic: on a $1bn loan, 200bp is $20M a year, real money at scale. In the upper middle market it narrows to about 500bp spread versus 325–350bp in an open BSL market, so large borrowers flip back to syndicated when it reopens. - Allocation: Churchill splits each deal pro rata across about 50 vehicles (dedicated senior, dedicated junior funds that "signed up" for 100–300bp more, equity co-invest), so a $300M deal becomes many small positions and no fund cherry-picks. It turns down 80–90% of what originators source.

Business significance / value. The sponsor buys certainty: no rating process, no syndication flex, one price that holds, and a lender who can approve another $50–150M in two weeks. The lender captures spread, upfront fees and covenant control. Churchill's sourcing edge is that it is often an LP in the sponsor's funds, so the sponsor keeps calling even after being turned down; its parent TIAA supplies "permanent capital".

Forces & impact. Competition from new entrants ("on fund one") and the reopening BSL market compress spreads and loosen terms at the top end. Longer PE hold periods (now above six years versus a historical four or five, per Gornick) slow repayments and push lenders into "amend and extend" or dividend recaps. Regional banks were constrained after SVB, ceding the lower tiers. Second-order: scale wins. A lender that can offer more than today's need signals it can fund the next five years of growth.

With vs. without. Without unitranche, a sponsor in an auction must coordinate two lenders who disagree on price and intercreditor terms, and loses to a rival with a cleaner package. With it, one lender holds 5.5–7x of leverage, so its recovery depends entirely on its own underwriting; there is no junior lender below it to absorb the first loss.

Applies when / Breaks when. Works for PE-backed, cash-generative middle-market companies where speed and flexibility are worth 150–250bp. Breaks when the lender "taps out" and can't fund the next draw (the borrower's risk), when the next owner asks for a more aggressive structure and the incumbent declines, and when competition strips covenants in the upper tier.

Channel example. What is Private Credit? | Direct Lending Explained (Alona Gornick, ex-Bank of America gaming banker and Oaktree high-yield analyst, now Churchill).

Counterpoint. Gornick is pitching her firm to wealth clients, and "low loss rates" describe a market that has not been through a full default cycle at its current size. Being an LP in the sponsor's funds is a sourcing edge and a conflict: a lender courting the next fund allocation may be slow to enforce against that sponsor. Unitranche "efficiency" also concentrates 5.5–7x in one lender, and her own earlier career story (Oaktree's Harrah's bonds primed by an LBO, §14) is what happens when documents are loose.

Links. tiger sisters private capital 101 (the sponsor's side of the same deal), canon brandenburger nalebuff coopetition (direct lenders compete for deals but need each other in clubs).

9 · Asset-based lending (and the double-pledge failure)

What it is. In asset-based lending (ABL) the lender is repaid by a pool of assets (consumer loans, leases, invoices, purchase orders, receivables) rather than by the borrower's overall earnings. Direct lending to a company relies on "the good faith and credit" of that company; ABL relies on the collateral pool (Findley). Gornick draws the same line from the other side: a direct lender's "security" is the enterprise value of the whole business, which can be mostly goodwill, while ABL has hard collateral.

How it works. Findley's underwriting is a transition matrix. Of current loans, how many go 30 days delinquent; of those, how many cure, stay, or roll to 60. Iterate to a lifetime default estimate, set the loan-to-value and rate off that estimate times a safety multiple, and lend where you get your money back even under stress. She did this as a stochastic process at Morgan Stanley ABS-CDO research and now does it on $10–40M loans. Her formative trade (Third Point, 2009): take a $100M Alt-A mortgage bond downgraded to D, have a rating agency re-tranche it into a 60% AAA senior piece and a 40% mezzanine piece, keep the mezz at about 10 cents with a 5% coupon on par. Two years of coupons (5 + 5 = 10 cents) returned the purchase price, and anything after was profit. She sanity-checked the dealer's deeply pessimistic assumptions against a chart showing 97% of mortgage defaulters default by month 60, so a pool that had paid for five years was unlikely to default en masse.

Business significance / value. ABL finances fintechs, auto lenders and specialty finance companies that are too volatile for cash-flow lending but hold predictable asset pools. Findley's further point is that returns and AUM are inversely correlated. A $500M fund can live on $20–40M deals that the $100bn managers cannot staff, which is her pitch for small managers.

Forces & impact. Collateral illiquidity forces long lockups. Findley left Third Point because 90-day investor liquidity could not hold illiquid loans, which is the same mismatch that later hit BDCs (§12). The failure mode is collateral that does not exist. First Brands (Gatto's summary): a founder-owned (100%) auto aftermarket parts maker (wipers and the like) built by acquisitions funded in the syndicated loan market. A routine refinancing asked for more debt than it had; existing holders were positive, but new, more sophisticated eyes stalled the process, the loans fell from about 96–100 into the 30s, and it filed. The same receivables had been pledged to several lenders ("hidden factoring"), about $2.3bn of assets "evaporated", and total liabilities including off-balance-sheet financing ran to roughly $10–11bn. Exposure surfaced at Jefferies' Point Bonita fund and UBS O'Connor (reportedly about 30% of one portfolio). Lenders requested a Deloitte quality-of-earnings report, the $6bn refinancing failed, and the company filed Chapter 11 on Sept. 28. Gatto expects hundreds of millions in bankruptcy costs. Tricolor, a subprime used-car lender, filed Chapter 7. Zions ($50M write-off) and Western Alliance disclosed fraud-linked loans the same week. Gatto's lesson is procedural: a red flag (debt sitting in SPVs, §6) doesn't mean a bad deal, it means ask more questions. Silver Point analyzed the loans and had no exposure.

With vs. without. ABL works only if the lender verifies and controls the collateral: lockboxes, UCC filings, field audits. Without verification it becomes unsecured lending at secured spreads. Jen's analogy: one house, two mortgages, two banks.

Applies when / Breaks when. Applies to granular, data-rich pools with long performance histories. Breaks under correlated defaults (the CDO lesson Findley lived through, where pooled assets were not independent) and under fraud, which surfaces "when something goes wrong" (§18).

Channel example. Private Credit 101: Asset-Based Lending feat. Keri Findley. First Brands Bankruptcy, Gold at Record Highs. The best explanation of why everyone is worried about Private Credit (short). Gatto's First Brands account in Distressed Debt 101 with the GOAT.

Counterpoint. Findley's returns (mid-20s unlevered IRR at Third Point, "30s" net in one quarter at Tacora) are self-reported, and a single strong quarter says little about risk. One video says First Brands failed to refinance "$6 million"; it was $6bn. The hosts frame First Brands as possible fraud, and on air it was still alleged. Gatto's "you could have spotted it" is hindsight from a firm that passed; the lenders who stayed in also had the documents.

Links. canon akerlof market for lemons (lenders can't see collateral quality, so the bad borrowers self-select), acumen/case-03-carvana.md (auto-loan securitization).

10 · PIK (payment-in-kind) interest

What it is. PIK lets a borrower pay interest by adding it to the loan balance instead of paying cash. Kristen calls it the buy-now-pay-later of interest. A PIK toggle lets the borrower choose cash or PIK period by period.

How it works. $100 at 10% means $10 cash a year. PIK it once and you owe $110; next year's interest is $11, then $12.10, compounding the principal. The Bloomberg data (four years of tracking, so the "four-year high" is a since-records-began high) shows PIK use in private credit rising from about 7.7% to almost 12%. The share of that which is "bad PIK" rose from about 18% to roughly 50%. Bad PIK means the borrower elected it after the deal closed, rather than it being structured in at signing. "Good PIK" is lender-dictated structure: senior lenders cap cash interest to juniors, so a junior tranche might be 10% cash plus 5% PIK.

Business significance / value. For the borrower, PIK conserves cash in a squeeze. For a BDC, PIK counts as income but brings in no cash, so it inflates reported earnings and can fund dividends that are not covered by cash (Indap: analysts back it out). For the sponsor, PIK buys time for the equity option. Medallia shows the limit. A Thoma Bravo 2021 LBO had been PIKing; its lenders (Apollo, Blackstone and others) refused to allow more and demanded new equity or the keys. Thoma Bravo handed over the company.

Forces & impact. Rate rises on floating-rate debt raise cash interest exactly when EBITDA is under pressure, and PIK is the release valve. Second-order: PIK delays defaults (smoothing reported default rates), raises the eventual loss given default, because the claim has grown while the asset hasn't, and makes BDC NAVs lag reality. Gatto's view of the accommodation game: experienced lenders give "tender loving care" (amendments, PIK, more sponsor equity) to deals they believe in, but get paid for it in fees and a higher rate, and move fast to de-risk the ones they don't. The question for any PIK election is which of those two the lender thinks it is.

With vs. without. Without PIK, stressed borrowers default sooner and lenders take control earlier, with more value left. With unlimited PIK, a zombie borrower compounds its debt until there is nothing left to recover. The canary in the coal mine that Kristen remembers from 2006–07 is back.

Applies when / Breaks when. PIK is benign when structured in at signing for a growth company expected to refinance. It is a distress signal when borrower-elected after closing on a no-growth business.

Channel example. What does the rise in PIK loans mean for Private Credit? (podcast). Why a SaaS Company Default (Medalla) is actually a WIN for Private Credit (short). Indap in Pt 3. Gatto on paid accommodation in Distressed Debt 101.

Counterpoint. The Medallia short calls the default a "win" for private credit because big lenders took control. That is spin. A default the lender forces is still a loss against par, and the short admits that smaller managers without restructuring teams or "fancy lawyers" are the worry. The PIK statistics' denominator (which deals, whose dataset) isn't given on air. The tracker is likely Lincoln International via Bloomberg, which should be checked before reuse.

Links. canon sterman business dynamics (stock-and-flow: PIK is an unpaid flow accumulating into the debt stock).

11 · LBO leverage then vs now: Caesars, TXU, EA

What it is. A leveraged buyout (LBO) funds an acquisition mostly with debt borrowed by the target and repaid from its cash flows. The repo has the mechanics (tiger sisters private capital 101). The channel adds the cross-cycle comparison and the sponsor-side economics.

How it works.

Caesars (2006–08) TXU (2007) EA (2025)
Enterprise value $30bn ~$45bn $55bn
Equity ~$6bn (Apollo 1.325 + TPG 1.325 + ~30 co-investors ~3.5) ~$8bn (KKR, TPG, GS Capital) ~$36bn (Silver Lake, PIF, Affinity)
Equity % ~20% <20% ~65%
Debt $24bn: $7bn bank loans, $6bn bridge-to-HY, $6.5bn CMBS, $4.5bn legacy Harrah's ~$36bn ($24bn senior loans, $11bn HY) $20bn, one bank (JPM)
Leverage ~8x ($24bn / $3bn EBITDA) ~8.5x LTM ~7.5x
Outcome Bankrupt 2015 Bankrupt (Energy Future Holdings) —

Why EA needs so much equity: at 20x EBITDA purchase price and banks lending 7–8x, debt covers at most 7.5/20 ≈ 37.5% of the price. The rest, roughly 62.5%, must be equity, which matches the 65% reported. That is also why PE historically avoided tech: high multiples break the math. For scale, a core middle-market buyout today runs about 5–5.5x (4x senior plus 1–2x junior), or up to about 7x in a unitranche (Gornick, §8), so these mega-deals sit at the top of the range. Sponsor fee extraction at Caesars: $100M each to Apollo and TPG as "consulting" at close, plus about 1% of EBITDA (~$30M/yr) in monitoring fees, typically followed by a termination fee at exit.

Business significance / value. Equity returns (targeted at 22–27% IRR at Caesars) come from three levers: EBITDA growth, multiple expansion, and debt paydown. Caesars paid down only $185M from 2014–16 because it kept borrowing to stay alive, so the third lever ran backwards. Co-invest beat club deals after Caesars because Apollo and TPG fought over control. One sponsor now runs the company and LPs co-invest without paying 2-and-20 (EA has one operator, Silver Lake).

Forces & impact. Cheap debt and fundraising surges push deal size (2005: Toys R Us $7bn, SunGard $11.4bn; 2007: TXU). Today the drivers are sovereign wealth equity and single-bank or private-credit commitments. Second-order: a large equity cushion protects lenders, but it also lowers sponsor IRR, which invites PIK, preferred structures, or fee layering to rebuild returns. Kristen suspects Silver Lake has a preferential slice.

With vs. without. Thin equity (TXU, Caesars) means any shock (energy prices, 2008) wipes out equity and moves straight into creditor fights. A 65% cushion means the equity takes the first $36bn of losses. That's why "same leverage multiple" does not mean "same risk".

Applies when / Breaks when. Debt/EBITDA comparisons apply when EBITDA is stable. They break when the purchase multiple is the risk: at 20x, a fall to 12x erases about 40% of enterprise value, which still sits inside EA's equity. The same fall at 8x equity would not.

Channel example. Eerie Similarities Between Record Setting 2025 LBO (EA) and 2007 TXU LBO. Largest LBO EVER!!! Harbinger of another 2008? (short). Caesars LBO (Pt 1/3). Skechers' $9B deal shows why in LBOs, cash isn't always king... A Primer on Rollover Equity (short).

Counterpoint. The hosts compare a regulated utility with a commodity hedge (TXU) to a gaming franchise (EA) as if leverage meant the same thing in both. It doesn't. They also do not ask whether EA's $36bn includes rolled-over existing stakes (PIF was already an EA shareholder), which would mean less new cash than headlined. The Skechers short shows how common that is: 3G offered holders $63 cash or $57 plus one unlisted equity unit, with rollover capped at 20% so 3G keeps 80%. Rolled equity counts toward the cushion but is not new money. Paramount/WBD ("$25bn buying $110bn", about 7x) is called an LBO in substance. That's fair, but it's an analogy, not a classification.

Links. tiger sisters private capital 101, canon jensen meckling agency theory (fees paid by the company to its owners).

12 · BDCs, semi-liquid vehicles & gating

What it is. Retail investors want liquidity; direct loans have none. Three wrappers bridge the gap (Private Credit: The Best Explanation): - A public BDC (business development company, a regulated vehicle lending to mid-size companies) lists on an exchange. Investors exit by selling shares to each other; the fund's cash is untouched, and the share price can sit far from NAV. - A non-traded BDC (Blackstone's BCRED, Blue Owl's private sister fund) is bought at NAV and redeemed through quarterly windows, typically capped around 5% of the fund. The manager may stop redemptions altogether. - An interval fund (Cliffwater is the example) is legally required to offer to repurchase a set slice of shares each period, so it cannot simply shut the door.

Gating means limiting or suspending redemptions when requests exceed the cap.

How it works. Leverage arithmetic (gating short; Kristen's version in the explainer): investors put in $100, the fund borrows $100, and it makes $200 of loans yielding about 8–9%. Illustration (not from the channel): loans at 10%, borrowing at 6%, gives 20 − 6 = $14, a 14% return on equity before fees. A 5% loss on the loan book is $10, or 10% of equity. Indap: public BDCs run roughly 1:1 debt to equity, non-traded ones no more than 2:1. What's in the big funds, per the hosts' reading of filings: borrowers with around $250M of EBITDA, and ~80% senior secured at Blue Owl versus ~95% at Blackstone and BlackRock.

The 2026 sequence on air, in order: - Blue Owl turned its non-traded BDC into a drawdown fund in February, returning cash only as assets are sold. The hosts read it partly as closing an arbitrage: redeem the private fund at par, buy the public sister at a ~20% discount to NAV. - Blackstone's BCRED received about $3.8bn of redemption requests; senior partners put in $155M of their own money and the fund met everything. - Oaktree also paid above its cap (about 8.5%), backed by parent Brookfield. BlackRock and Ares enforced their caps. Apollo capped redemptions on its $25bn BDC, and the hosts report Moody's stripped a KKR credit fund of its investment-grade rating. - A $25M BlackRock loan went from par to zero in three months, a "hangnail" against a multi-billion book (Jen) that still became a headline. - Boaz Weinstein (Saba Capital, the activist) bid 65–80 cents for the gated Blue Owl shares, which Kristen reads as a floor.

Kroboth adds two mechanics that shrink the scary numbers. First, investors over-request. If requests are pro-rated at 7%, asking for 100% returns seven times what asking for 20% does, so headline request figures overstate real demand for cash. Second, people redeem from the best funds first, the ones still paying out at or above NAV, which he calls everybody running for the cash machine.

Business significance / value. BDCs are how alternative asset managers reach retail, the "only real untapped market" (Indap). Institutions are near peak allocation, and public alt managers traded at about 40x forward earnings (Blackstone above $200bn market cap) on a story of growing from about $500bn to $1–1.5trn AUM each. Fees stack: the manager's cut plus the wealth adviser's, against 5–10bp at Vanguard or Fidelity. Jen frames the two readings: the cynic's (institutional money ran out, so retail backfills) and the fair one (private markets were the path to wealth for the connected, and access is overdue).

Forces & impact. Rates, software-sector stress (heavy BDC concentration in SaaS) and fraud headlines drive redemptions. Redemptions force gates, gates cause panic, and panic drives more requests. Kristen was gated in Blackstone's BREIT in 2022 while moving and buying a house: wet-signature letters by mail, and a year to get out. Second-order: the gate protects remaining holders from fire sales (the SVB lesson: depositors ran Friday and the bank was gone by Sunday), but it breaks the retail expectation of liquidity, which threatens the 401(k) channel. Kristen's counter: a 401(k) is the right home, because it's the money nobody touches. The mismatch was obvious years ago, Kroboth says, and well-run managers hold cash buffers, credit lines and a map of what takes 24 months versus five years to liquidate.

With vs. without. Without a gate, the first redeemers are paid at stale NAV and the last are left holding the worst loans, a classic run. With a gate, everyone shares the illiquidity, which is what the documents said all along. The interval fund is the uncomfortable middle: by law it must keep paying out, so in a rush it may have to sell loans when locking the door would serve holders better.

Applies when / Breaks when. Works for long-horizon investors who never need the money (Harvard, CalSTRS). Breaks for doctors and dentists sold "low risk, great returns", and whenever NAV lags secondary prices enough that redeeming at NAV is a free option (the public-private discount). Kroboth doubts that arbitrage works at scale, and secondary buyers stand ready to buy stakes in gated funds at a discount.

Channel example. Private Credit: The Best Explanation of Exactly What's Happening (structures, caps, Kroboth). Private Credit Deep Dive: Is this 2008 all over again? (BCRED, BREIT, Weinstein). Private Credit GATING?!….WTF is Happening with Blue Owl, Blackstone, BlackRock and Morgan Stanley? (short). The BEST EXPLAINER... BCRED or OBDC (short). Indap in Pt 3.

Counterpoint. The leverage figures came partly from the hosts asking an AI. The legal cap for all BDCs has been 2:1 debt/equity since 2018, so the 1:1 public figure is practice, not a rule. The hosts say interval funds must allow "5 to 7%"; under the SEC's interval-fund rule the required periodic repurchase offer is 5–25% of shares, set by the fund. The "40%" Blue Owl redemption figure from the gating short was flagged on air as "something like that", and the KKR downgrade is reported, not shown. Pass 1 of this note carried the bidder as "Eisenberg"; the full episode names Boaz Weinstein. Indap's view (correction, not catastrophe) is the more defensible one: fund leverage of 1–2x is modest next to 2008 bank and CDO leverage.

Links. canon perrow normal accidents (tight coupling: redemption terms tied to illiquid assets), canon thaler sunstein nudge (Indap: gates as a forced nudge against selling at the bottom), wss private markets wealth (the wealth-channel distribution side).

13 · The insurer balance-sheet model (and related-party risk)

What it is. Asset managers buy or build life insurers because insurers collect premiums today against payouts decades away and need long-dated, yield-paying assets. The manager can originate those assets itself: a private equity deal, financed by its own private credit, sold to its own insurer, earning fees at every step. Apollo/Athene is the template.

How it works. Capital charges (Jen's figures): investment-grade bonds about 1–2% (about 50x leverage on the insurer's capital), riskier loans 6–7%, common equity about 30%. Investments in related parties require more capital and disclosure, and they are capped. Delaware Life, an insurer tied to Mark Walter's TWG and managed by Guggenheim, reported $1.4bn of related-party investments, then after a DOJ probe revised the figure to $17bn, about 39% of its portfolio and well above the cap. Walter bought the Lakers at a $10bn valuation in October and agreed to sell within the year at $12.5bn to Josh Kushner (Thrive) and Bob Iger. The market inferred a forced unwind to repay insurer loans. Jen also reports a related insurer group restructuring away its voting stake 18 months before the subpoenas, which reclassified about $2.5bn as unaffiliated, and political donations tied to a Kansas insurance-regulation delay. All of this is reported, not charged.

Business significance / value. This model is the cheapest, stickiest funding source in private credit and a large part of the post-2008 growth of alt managers. Value is captured three times: origination fees (the bank arm), management fees (the asset manager), and spread (the insurer).

Forces & impact. State-level insurance regulation, capital-charge arbitrage, and the illiquidity of what the insurer holds. Second-order: the insurer's policyholders become unknowing lenders to the manager's own deals, and risk becomes concentrated in correlated counterparties. Kristen draws the CDO parallel of assumed zero correlation.

With vs. without. Without captive insurers, private credit would have to raise every dollar from third parties at market terms. With undisclosed related-party lending, the insurer "really just owned Mark Walter" (FT reader comment quoted by Jen), so policyholder security depends on trophy-asset values.

Applies when / Breaks when. Works with arm's-length assets and honest disclosure. Breaks when assets are related-party, illiquid, and must be sold in a down market, and when the regulator is captured.

Channel example. Why the Lakers Sale to Kushner & Iger is ACTUALLY the Craziest Private Credit Scandal of the Year. The TRUTH about the LA Lakers $12.5Bn Sale (short).

Counterpoint. Jen labels the episode "conspiracy corner" herself. The forced-sale thesis is inference: a 25% markup in a year on a scarce NBA franchise also fits an opportunistic seller. No charges had been filed on air. The Madoff framing is clickbait, and the hosts concede no Ponzi is alleged.

Links. canon akerlof market for lemons, canon jensen meckling agency theory (manager vs policyholder).

14 · Liability management & creditor-on-creditor violence

What it is. Liability management exercises (LMEs) are out-of-court transactions in which a distressed company and some creditors restructure debt in ways that leave other creditors worse off. Three names for one thing (Gatto): LME is the lawyers' term, creditor-on-creditor violence the press's, and "position enhancing transactions" a law firm's attempt at spin that never caught on. Lenders hold only contractual rights; the board's fiduciary duty runs to shareholders. So anything the documents don't forbid is fair game (Caesars Palace Coup, read on air).

How it works. Gatto's worked uptier (Distressed Debt 101). A sponsor buys a company for $3bn: $1bn equity, $2bn broadly syndicated senior secured loan, held mostly by CLOs. In the old mindset every holder of that loan was a musketeer, one for all. The document says no new debt can rank ahead of or alongside it, but like most loan documents it can be amended by a simple majority (sometimes two-thirds). 1. The company underperforms and needs $200M of new money. 2. A majority of lenders votes to amend the document to allow $1.2bn of new debt senior to the existing loan. So far everyone is diluted equally. 3. The same majority provides the $1.2bn. $200M goes to the company; the other $1bn buys back the majority's own old loans at a small discount (say 95). 4. Result: the majority now holds $1.2bn of super-senior debt. The minority holds the remaining $1bn of old loan, now junior to $1.2bn, and its price drops from about 85 to 30. Same company, same cash flows; only the ranking changed.

For a distressed fund on the winning side the arithmetic is better still: buy the loan at 60, exchange it at a discount into 85 of new money that ranks ahead of everyone, and that 85 behaves like par.

The Caesars playbook, the template, in order: 1. Open-market buybacks of bonds at discount (50 cents retires $1). Efficient, but it creates cancellation-of-debt income, taxable, which the company could not pay. The 2009 stimulus let it be deferred (the hosts say "got rid of"; it was a deferral). 2. Uptier exchange: offer holders of $100 of later-maturing debt about $80 of new debt that is senior, with a higher coupon and a later maturity. Participants move up; non-participants are pushed down. 3. Drop-down to a clean affiliate: Apollo and TPG created Caesars Growth Partners (CGP), which had no legacy debt, and had it buy assets from the OpCo. Planet Hollywood plus one other casino went for $350M, with a stated value of $360M that management projected to reach $830M within three years. The online gaming business went for $525M, projected at $820M. The projected gain was about $775M (470 + 295 ≈ 765, close enough), and the projections were shown to the board one month after closing. Evercore's fairness opinion did not update for Britney Spears' residency. A later four-property sale targeted $2bn cash and cost the OpCo $3bn of revenue and $700M of EBITDA. Junior bonds fell to 12 cents. 4. Guarantee release: OpCo debt was guaranteed by the parent only while the OpCo was wholly owned. Apollo sold a minority stake (options on OpCo shares) to friendly investors, so the OpCo was no longer wholly owned, and argued the guarantee fell away.

Gornick saw the precursor from inside Oaktree: it bought newly issued Harrah's bonds, and shortly after, the buyout put "a massive amount" of new debt ahead of them through an opening in the documents.

Later variants: J.Crew (a provision let the company move valuable assets, its intellectual property, away from lenders' collateral) and Serta (a non-pro-rata uptier). Indap's modern form: in a cov-lite loan-only structure, two groups of equal first-lien lenders bid to provide rescue financing; the winner rolls up its old debt into a new super-senior class and the losers drop "four steps" back.

Business significance / value. LMEs transfer value from non-participating creditors to equity and to participating creditors, legally if the documents allow and short of fraudulent conveyance. Value is captured by whoever has the best lawyers, the most capital to fund the new money, and the earliest seat at the table. Funds on the right side post "supercharged" returns; the cost is paid by passive holders: CLOs, small managers, retail BDCs. Gatto's blunt advice to the losers is "Know what you agree to." LMEs also create trades: when Bausch Health's secured bonds sold off on fear of being LME'd behind the term loan, Silver Point bought them, judging the feared transaction would not happen.

Forces & impact. Gatto gives three causes. A cultural change after 2008: sponsors used to boast that no senior secured lender lost money with them, and after 2008 protecting their own LPs came first. Sponsors also hired the best lawyers to build borrower-friendly escape hatches into documents. And small lenders couldn't push back: a CLO taking $5–10M of a $1bn deal won't read a 300-page agreement or demand changes, because it is being "done a favor" by getting any allocation. Add cov-lite documents, loan-only stacks, and big managers on every side of every deal (Oaktree was there to "drink the blood of Apollo" and is also a PE firm). Second-order effects: first-lien recoveries fall (about 80 to about 60 cents, Moody's via Indap); borrowers put aggressive funds on disqualified-lender lists (First Brands blacklisted Apollo, partly for its LME reputation and partly because Apollo owns rival Tenneco and would have seen the data room); lenders now negotiate anti-LME "blockers". Gatto expects LMEs to stay "part of the docs" as long as capital chases deals, and says it is much more a syndicated-loan problem than a private-credit one.

With vs. without. Without LMEs, a distressed company files and the absolute priority rule distributes value by rank. With them, rank is renegotiated before court, and seniority becomes a starting position rather than an entitlement. In 2008 CLOs survived because they were senior secured and everything below took the pain first (Gatto); a "senior secured" lender who wakes up behind $1.2bn of new debt has no such cushion. In Caesars, the courts and an involuntary filing by junior creditors ultimately reversed much of it.

Applies when / Breaks when. LMEs work when documents are loose, a majority can be co-opted, and the lender group is large and anonymous (syndicated loans, bonds). They break in court when the transfer looks like fraudulent conveyance, when the fairness process is visibly conflicted, or when excluded creditors band together, as Oaktree and others did with an involuntary petition. Serta shows how fragile the legal ground is. Judge Jones (Southern District of Texas) approved the uptier and the company emerged on that basis. Jones later resigned over an undisclosed relationship with a lawyer who appeared before him. Then the Fifth Circuit ruled on New Year's Eve (2024) that the deal did not fit the document's open-market-purchase exception. They also break in small private clubs: Gornick and Kroboth argue that two to eight like-minded lenders who will meet again rarely turn on each other, and Kroboth avoids the issue by being sole lender. His reasoning: LMEs are common "because it's possible".

Channel example. Distressed Debt 101 with the GOAT (Gatto's uptier, Serta, J.Crew, Bausch). Distressed Debt 102: When Debt Investors Turn On Each Other | Caesars Pt 2/3. What is Private Credit? | Direct Lending Explained (Harrah's priming). Why did First Brands BLACKLIST Apollo from its list of lenders? (short). Financial Times reporter: How Private Credit Has Changed Since 2008…and Gotten Riskier (short). Indap in Pt 3.

Counterpoint. The hosts treat Apollo as a near-cartoon villain while admitting it was "vindicated": Caesars did recover once the debt was gone, and the recovery went to the creditors. LMEs can also preserve going-concern value that a premature filing would destroy, part of why Gatto calls them a fascinating subject rather than an evil. Indap calls true creditor-on-creditor fights "still relatively limited". The bigger driver of lower recoveries is simply that loans now form more of the stack. Kroboth's claim that Apollo is now "much more boring" comes from a peer, not an audit, and the club argument is untested in a deep downturn.

Links. canon jensen meckling agency theory (asset substitution and claim dilution, the debt-side agency costs), canon schelling strategy of conflict (coalitions and commitment among creditors), canon axelrod evolution of cooperation (why cooperation holds in repeated private clubs and unravels among anonymous syndicate holders).

15 · Distressed investing, valuation fights & bankruptcy

What it is. Three different things (Caesars Pt 2). Distressed investing is a strategy: buy debt someone else lent, now trading at a material discount (80, 70, even 10 cents), and profit either when it recovers toward par or by converting it into control. Restructuring is the negotiation to save a struggling company: asset sales, exchanges, LMEs. Bankruptcy is court: Chapter 11 reorganizes and keeps the company running; Chapter 7 liquidates it (First Brands filed 11; Tricolor filed 7). Gatto's framing: about 80% of the skill set is ordinary corporate investing (industry, business, model); the other 20% is the bankruptcy code, documents and negotiation.

How it works. Gatto's strategy spectrum (Distressed Debt 101): - Pull to par. Buy at 82, clip the coupon, get repaid at 100 because the company never files. The return beats a loan bought at 98 for the same credit. - Distress for control. Buy debt you expect to become the equity. Men's Wearhouse (Gatto groups it with Jos. A. Bank; both sat under Tailored Brands) in COVID: senior secured debt at 30–50 cents, below what Silver Point thought liquidating inventory and owned real estate would return. Downside: cost back plus a little. Upside: convert to equity, inject liquidity, and ride the pent-up demand for weddings, tux rentals and new work clothes. It worked. - Capital-structure relative value. Two bonds of one company trade together, but the documents make one better. Lehman had bonds with a double-dip claim (two recoveries from the estate). The dispute settled at 1.8x the normal bonds' recovery without a trial, and the other side agreeing to 1.8 told you who would have won. The edge is finding a lawyer who isn't conflicted, since every big firm represents someone in the case. - LME plays. Position for, or against, a feared transaction (§14).

Apollo and TPG at Caesars ran distress for control too: about $70M for $300M face of Planet Hollywood's junior mortgage debt, converted into a controlling equity stake by early 2010. Debt as quasi-equity: Paulson bought Caesars unsecured bonds at about 66 cents and swapped about $1.1bn face for 16% of the parent at a $4.5bn equity value. Check: 0.16 × $4.5bn = $720M, against a cost of about 0.66 × $1.1bn ≈ $726M, so he swapped at almost exactly his cost basis.

Valuation fights. Gatto's example: $500M of secured debt, $200M of unsecured bonds you bought at 40, betting the bonds get a recovery, probably in equity. The judge values the company at $400M. That is less than the $500M secured claim, so secured lenders get 100% of the new equity and the bonds get zero. Two years later the company sells for $800M, enough to have covered all $700M of debt. You were right on value and still got nothing. Most fights settle (say 90/10) before a judge rules.

The bankruptcy toolkit. In Chapter 11 a company can reject or assume leases, renegotiate union contracts, and emerge with much less debt, often with some creditors as the new owners, effectively the new private equity sponsor. Filing also freezes maneuvering, like someone shouting "Uno". At Caesars, junior creditors (Oaktree et al.) filed an involuntary petition to freeze Apollo's moves. Outcome: about two years of litigation, $273M in estate fees ($79M to Kirkland & Ellis alone), emergence October 2017. Second-lien bonds went from cents to 65 at emergence to about 100 as Caesars and VICI stock rallied, roughly $5bn of value. Elliott made about $1bn.

Business significance / value. Distressed funds supply liquidity to forced sellers (hung bridges bought at about 80 cents in 2008; Third Point buying forced-sold paper in 2009) and are often the eventual owners. Gatto's defense against the "vulture" label: distressed funds fund rescues that avoid bankruptcy (capital solutions, §16), bring in restructuring advisers, and use the code to cut debt so the business can hire and grow again. The holding period is the edge. Private equity's 7–10 year lockups let it wait; hedge funds with short redemption terms may be forced to sell at the bottom. Blackstone held Hilton through the crisis and made about $10bn.

Forces & impact. Kroboth (Northwall; the "three rules" short is his, not Gatto's): big managers now raise dislocation funds that can only be drawn after preset market triggers, so risk reprices fast and the chance to deploy a lot at 70 is brief. A good distress cycle needs a sudden, unexpected shock; a foreseeable maturity wall gets refinanced, extended and nibbled away by credit funds, capital-solutions funds and credit-secondaries funds. He waited 15 years for one. When a real dislocation comes, LPs struggle to allocate new money because their other holdings are falling (the denominator problem), so committed capital wins. Europe's distressed market is too small to be an asset class, and the famous US distressed shops (Oaktree among them) have become broad credit platforms. Gatto's forecast for the turn sorts lenders into three groups. Cycle-tested funds with workout teams will keep lending when others stop and outperform. Decent underwriters without workout staff will pause. Funds run by people who never saw a cycle will fail to raise again and disappear.

With vs. without. Without distressed buyers, forced sellers' prices fall further and companies are liquidated instead of reorganized. With them, a default is "the beginning of a potential restructuring" (Medallia short), not the end. Without a valuation process, the senior class would simply take the company; with one, junior classes get a forum, and a costly fight.

Applies when / Breaks when. Works when you have capital, legal resources, and time. Breaks when you are on the wrong side of the documents or the valuation ruling, when your own liquidity is short, or when you are too early, paying carry while waiting for a cycle that is being refinanced away.

Channel example. Distressed Debt 101 with the GOAT: Michael Gatto (strategies, Men's Wearhouse, Lehman double dip, valuation fights). Distressed Debt 102 (Pt 2/3). Private Credit: The Best Explanation of Exactly What's Happening and its clip CIO of $3Bn Private Credit Firm on THREE RULES for Making Money in Distressed Investing (Kroboth). Private Equity's Blueprint... (Pt 1/3) (hung bridges, the Rowan "you want chaos" ethos).

Counterpoint. Pass 1 of this note attributed the dislocation-fund argument to Gatto; the full episode shows it is Kroboth's. The Planet Hollywood figures don't reconcile: the hosts say "50 cents on the dollar" but also $70M for $300M face, which is about 23 cents. One number is wrong. Gatto's heroes-not-vultures pitch is self-description, and the valuation-fight example cuts both ways: secured holders who win a low valuation capture the later upside. The "blood in the streets" career lesson is survivorship-biased; the hedge funds forced to sell at the bottom are the other half of the story. Kristen argues lawyers are well placed to move into distressed; Gatto, who has no law degree, says you can learn the legal side on the job.

Links. canon klarman margin of safety (forced selling creates price ≠ value; Klarman's Baupost is a distressed shop), canon mauboussin success equation (luck of timing in distressed returns), canon fisher ury getting to yes (most valuation fights end in negotiated splits; know your alternative to a ruling).

16 · Capital solutions / special situations ("credit opportunities")

What it is. Lending into situations too complex, urgent or unusual for a bank, a direct lender or a mezzanine lender. Kroboth places it on a ladder: plain direct lending (reasonable leverage), unitranche (more), mezzanine (closer to equity), then special situations, which his firm rebrands "credit opportunities". The defining feature is situational complexity, usually with urgency. Distressed buys someone else's debt in the secondary market; capital solutions originates new senior debt.

How it works. Kroboth's examples (Northwall, ~$3bn): - Project North. A UK industrial company. A PE buyer had chased it for 18 months; one of its high street lenders dropped out four weeks before closing. Northwall decided fast and closed on time, for extra economics. The risk was low; the price was for speed and certainty. - Consumer tail portfolios. Hundreds of millions of defaulted, already worked-out bank receivables (overdrafts and similar) where the customer is on a ten-year payment plan. The hard work is done; what is left is a long annuity that the owner sells for liquidity. - Legal assets. Not single-case litigation funding, which is venture-like (some zeros, some 5x), but loans to law firms secured on their whole case portfolio, structured as credit: downside protection, contractual return, fixed maturity. Last money in, first money out of any case revenue, repaid in about five years. One loan of about $186M against a book that could produce $1–2bn if every case won. The firm claims its book is worth 800, he thinks 200, he lends 30. The risk isn't losing cases (the portfolio diversifies that) but that lawyers are poor at running a business and run out of money. One case in that portfolio was the Mariana dam disaster in Brazil, which brought claims against BHP and Vale in English courts. - Terms. The borrower trades price and structure for speed and certainty. Pay more, fine, but no compromise on covenants, downside protection or EBITDA add-back limits.
