Northwall lost a deal two weeks before the episode because the intermediary called its terms "not market"; his reply was that the only willing lender is the market.

Business significance / value. This is where distressed expertise went in a decade without much distress. Kroboth's line, "Cap Solutions is the new distressed", and Gatto's description of capital solutions lending as being welcomed by the company and sponsor because it solves a problem, say the same thing. Returns come from complexity premia and fees, not from betting on default. Goldman closed its famous special situations group in favor of more scalable direct lending.

Forces & impact. Complex deals need closed-end, locked-up funds: a tariff-refund monetization or a law-firm loan can take 12–24 months and can never be traded out of. Legal-asset returns are uncorrelated with markets, which is the allocation pitch (0–10% of his fund). Second-order: as plain private credit gets crowded, borrowers who want plain-market loose terms at slightly higher prices drift into this niche; disciplined lenders wait them out, which caps fund size (his "why we're $3bn, not $10bn").

With vs. without. Without this capital, a PE deal dies when a bank drops out, and a law firm or a holder of a defaulted-loan tail has nowhere to turn. With it, those situations close, at a price, and the lender controls the outcome as sole lender rather than hoping a syndicate behaves (§14).

Applies when / Breaks when. Works when complexity, not credit quality, is what keeps other lenders away, and when the lender can hold to maturity. Breaks when "special situations" becomes a license to do anything, which Kroboth admits is why the label got a bad name, and when complexity hides plain bad credit.

Channel example. Private Credit: The Best Explanation of Exactly What's Happening (Fabian Kroboth, Northwall Capital). Gatto on capital solutions in Distressed Debt 101.

Counterpoint. Every example is a winner told by the manager, and "we turn down loose deals" is standard marketing. Legal-asset lending carries duration and ethics risk (financiers' influence over claims) that the episode doesn't discuss. His claim that big managers have planned for every liquidity scenario is reassurance from a peer, not evidence.

Links. professional services leverage (why law firms are cash-hungry partnerships), canon klarman margin of safety (lending 30 against an asset you value at 200).

17 · Credit default swaps (CDS)

What it is. A CDS is insurance on a borrower's default. The buyer pays a running premium (the CDS spread); the seller pays out if the borrower defaults. You don't need to own the bonds to buy protection, so CDS can be a hedge or an outright short on a company's credit. Carissa's origin story: CDS was built to make bondholders whole. If a bond recovers 40 in bankruptcy, protection pays the other 60, so the holder gets back par. It is now mostly a tool for views on credit and spread momentum.

How it works. Elliott at Caesars owned the debt and bought CDS against it. Sellers of short-dated protection reasoned a fresh cash infusion made bankruptcy impossible, which amounted to doubling down on their long. As bankruptcy approached, the protection rose in value. Apollo at First Brands was blacklisted as a lender (it owns rival Tenneco and has an LME reputation), bought CDS about a year early, and profited. Oracle: the OpenAI deal headlined at $300bn against OpenAI revenue of about $13bn (Jen's figure). Oracle's operating cash flow is about a quarter to a fifth of other hyperscalers', and its capex is debt-funded. Oracle lost about $315bn of market value from the peak, and its CDS became the market's "anti-AI trade": a liquid, cheap way to bet against AI capex, widening about 95bp against about 40bp for CDX IG.

Market structure (Credit Trading 101). The five-year contract is the liquid, "on-the-run" point. When Carissa traded (Frontier Communications bonds and CDS together), hundreds of single names traded, quoted from 1 to 10 years. Now the liquid products are the indices (CDX IG, CDX HY, a financials index coming), and single names trade only if they sit in an index. Prop desks and bond-vs-CDS basis traders have largely gone, bank CVA desks (which hedge the bank's own counterparty risk) remain, and some dealers have stopped making markets in single-name CDS altogether.

Business significance / value. CDS let banks and funds hedge concentrated loans and let skeptics express a view. Wider CDS feeds back into borrowing cost. Kristen notes Oracle can route around it through project finance, where a data center's own cash flows support the debt rather than Oracle's credit (the reverse of Meta, which borrows more cheaply as a corporate).

Forces & impact. CDS changes creditor incentives. A bondholder hedged with more protection than bonds is a net-short "empty creditor" who gains from default, which reshapes restructuring alliances (Caesars Pt 2). Reflexivity: buying a company's CDS widens its spreads and makes refinancing harder, so it is unclear which came first, the CDS or the egg. Kristen likens it to insuring a neighbour's house and then driving into it.

With vs. without. Without CDS, lenders could only hedge by selling the loan, and skeptics could only short equity. With CDS, credit risk is priced continuously, but someone with no economic interest in the company's survival can sit at the restructuring table.

Applies when / Breaks when. Works for liquid names with standardized contracts. Breaks in private credit (no CDS on a direct loan, hence the hunt for proxies like Oracle), for off-index single names where nobody makes a market, and when protection sellers cannot pay (AIG, 2008). The irony Kristen notes: a product invented so bondholders could protect a specific name now barely trades by name.

Channel example. Oracle CDS: the "Anti-AI Trade". Why Apollo Was Blacklisted By First Brands. Distressed Debt 102 (Pt 2/3). Credit Trading 101 (index vs single name). Related: The TRUTH about AI Data Centers (short): Nvidia backstopping about $250bn of a $527bn OpenAI build that sends it about $400bn of revenue, vendor credit that a CDS skeptic would price.

Counterpoint. Oracle CDS widening is partly hedging demand, so it measures how many people want an AI hedge as much as Oracle's default risk. The hosts say this, which is to their credit. The "$300bn" contract is multi-year and conditional, so set against one year of OpenAI revenue it overstates the mismatch. The data-center short's cost build is a creator's estimate.

Links. bloomberg terminal instrumentation (CDS, SOVR, WCDS, with no free equivalent), tiger sisters stock picking (2008 CDS), canon taleb black swan.

18 · Private credit vs 2008: same song, different instruments

What it is. The systemic question: is private credit's stress (gates, PIK, fraud, markdowns) a repeat of 2007–08 or a contained correction?

How it works. What rhymes. Too much money chasing too few deals, looser covenants, PIK toggles (back from 2006), opaque marks, retail distribution, and correlation assumed away (Kristen on CDOs: when it goes bad, it goes bad everywhere). Fraud surfaces when the cycle turns: Madoff, First Brands, Tricolor, the $2.6bn naked-short Treasury trader whose trade cost dealers about $250M when COVID moved rates 50bp against him (≈ $4.2M DV01 × 50bp ≈ $210M by Kristen's estimate). Indap: first lien means something "a lot different" now. What differs (Indap). Banks matter less and asset managers more. BDC leverage is 1–2x, not 30x. Corporate leverage in software is nothing like the 2006 housing bubble. In 2008 the underlying assets (subprime mortgages) were bad, re-levered through MBS, CDOs and CDO-squared. Kristen's 2007 CLO loans were mostly fine. The question is whether today's corporate loans resemble the loans of 2008 or the mortgages. Kristen's chain for 2008: "NINJA" loans (no income, job or assets) with adjustable rates, pooled into MBS, re-pooled into CDOs and CDO-squared, much of it held by the same banks that made the loans. Jen's: one web of institutions doing lending, liquidity and risk-taking at once. Today's equivalent sits in pensions, endowments, insurers and other funds with long horizons, so direct household exposure is small; the channels are pensions' marks, banks lending to funds, and sentiment spreading to public spreads. The new inversion: high-yield bonds (unsecured, larger BB issuers) yield about 6–8%, while "senior secured" leveraged and private loans yield 9–11%. That is not an arbitrage if the loan borrowers are worse companies, and they are. Smaller funds are easier to raise, so more money now flows to the lowest credit quality.

Business significance / value. For allocators: Global Alts private-credit meetings fell from 3,200 to 3,000, cooling rather than an exodus. Public credit meanwhile boomed: the record 2026 investment-grade issuance day (Amazon, Honeywell) was oversubscribed while BDCs were gating. Kristen's read is a flight to quality within credit. Amazon won't be "SaaS'd away"; a middle-market software borrower might. Data-center finance shows the same split: CoreWeave and Oracle reportedly couldn't fund one project, while Meta's Hyperion raised money against Meta's lease payments plus the building itself. Interest is shifting to long/short, relative value and macro. For the big alt managers: their valuations assumed the model survives a real credit cycle, which it hasn't faced since 2009. Indap's summary: correction, not catastrophe, but real pain for the sector.

Forces & impact. Retail and 401(k) access push supply. Sticky rates and SaaS disruption (AI) press on the software-heavy loan book. Gates educate investors the hard way. The $53bn-fund strategist's quip: private equity praising private credit is like Chick-fil-A's cows, because if you're in the credit, your equity has already been wiped out. Kroboth's diagnosis: a liquidity crisis set off by real but limited credit worries. The software scare triggered it, though some of the worst markdowns (the BlackRock fund) were old non-software loans. Jen adds the cynic's label for private marks, "volatility laundering", and the counter that patient capital sometimes really does work a loan out.

With vs. without. Without private credit, Gatto argues, bank pullbacks cascade into deeper downturns. His 2023 case: banks were stuck with the Twitter buyout debt they couldn't sell near par, SVB and other regional banks failed, and the Fed was raising rates into inflation; the large private lenders kept doing good deals, and nobody would bail out the ones that did bad deals. Without regulatory reach into private credit, the risk the 2008 reforms pushed out of banks sits with insurers and retail, and nobody has watched it through a downturn.

Applies when / Breaks when. The "contained" view holds if losses stay in software and mid-market loans and fund leverage stays modest. It breaks if insurer balance sheets (§13) or bank lending to private credit funds transmit losses, which is the inter-connection Indap says nobody yet knows. Both hosts end on the same split verdict in the deep dive: private credit probably isn't the domino, but oil, unemployment and a shakier property market could still produce a 2008-scale downturn around it.

Channel example. Private Credit Deep Dive: Is this 2008 all over again?. Private Credit: The Best Explanation of Exactly What's Happening. Distressed Debt 101 with the GOAT (Gatto's 2023 case). Financial Times Reporter TELLS ALL: Why Private Credit is Worse than Credit in 2008. Is Private Credit Fundraising OVER? We're LIVE from MIAMI!. Private Credit GATING?! (short). Chief Strategist of $53 Billion Hedge Fund (short).

Counterpoint. Kristen says 2008 corporate defaults "peaked at like 2%" and CLO investors did fine, and repeats it to Gatto, who doesn't correct her. Spec-grade defaults actually peaked near 10–14% in 2009 (Moody's/S&P loan and HY series). CLO senior tranches survived; equity and mezzanine took real losses, and the "investors made out like bandits" story applies to those who bought at the bottom. The Carlyle short's claim that "alternatives" is an archaic word, because listed US companies shrank from about 5,000 to about 3,500, is a sales pitch for retail allocation.

How the concepts connect

                              │

The loop that matters most: loose terms during tight spreads decide the recovery during wide spreads. Everything from PIK to LMEs is a cheap-money-era clause being exercised in a squeeze. Pass 2 adds a second loop: the size of the lender group decides how violent the squeeze gets. Anonymous syndicated holders (CLOs taking $5–10M of a $1bn loan) get uptiered; a sole lender or a small repeat club with maintenance covenants negotiates early (§8, §14, §16). And a third: whoever has committed, locked-up capital when sellers are forced sets the price, which is why dislocation funds and gates both exist (§12, §15).

Retrieval questions

  1. A company's 10-year Treasury rate falls 50bp after a tariff shock, but its own borrowing cost rises. How? The base rate fell on flight to safety, but the credit spread widened by more because default risk rose through input costs, demand and retaliation.
  2. Leverage is 4x against a 6x covenant. Without borrowing more, what EBITDA decline breaches it? A one-third decline: debt/EBITDA = 6 at EBITDA = 4/6 of the original. Breaches come from earnings, not just borrowing.
  3. Why does EA's 7.5x leverage carry less lender risk than TXU's 8.5x, beyond the 1-turn gap? A 65% equity cushion versus under 20%: equity absorbs the first ~$36bn of value loss. At 20x purchase and 7.5x debt, the math forces the cushion.
  4. A BDC reports rising net investment income while its cash interest receipts are flat. What do you suspect, and why does it matter for the dividend? PIK income is booked but not received, so the dividend may be funded by non-cash income and NAV may be overstated.
  5. Distinguish "good PIK" from "bad PIK". Good PIK is structured in at signing (often to fit seniors' cash caps). Bad PIK is elected by the borrower after closing to conserve cash, and it signals stress. The bad share rose from ~18% to ~50%.
  6. Why did Caesars' parent guarantee matter, and how did Apollo attack it? It gave OpCo creditors a claim on parent value. Selling a minority OpCo stake broke "wholly owned" status, which Apollo argued released the guarantee.
  7. You hold first-lien debt in a cov-lite, loan-only structure. Name two reasons your expected recovery is lower than a 2008 first-lien holder's. No junior bonds below to absorb losses, so recoveries are shared across a larger first-lien class; and uptier/roll-up LMEs can push non-participants behind a new super-senior class.
  8. Why can a gate be in the remaining investors' interest? It prevents fire-sale liquidation of illiquid loans to pay early redeemers at stale NAV. It shares the illiquidity instead of transferring losses to those who stay.
  9. Why might an investor buy a company's CDS rather than lend to it, and how can that change the company's fate? To short credit or hedge without exposure. Wider CDS raises refinancing costs (reflexivity), and net-short holders gain from default, which changes restructuring alliances.
  10. Paulson swapped $1.1bn face of Caesars bonds for 16% of a $4.5bn equity value. Was the swap rich or fair to him at the time? About fair at cost: 16% × 4.5 = $720M versus ~$726M paid (66c). He was buying optionality on a recovery, not a discount.
  11. Kroboth says a known maturity wall is a poor distressed setup. Why? A foreseeable problem gets refinanced, extended and nibbled by capital-solutions, secondaries and dislocation funds. Only a sudden shock forces real fire sales.
  12. Why is the insurer-owned asset manager model both private credit's best funding source and its likeliest transmission channel? Low capital charges (~1–2% on IG) and long-dated liabilities make it cheap, sticky funding. Related-party, illiquid assets concentrate policyholder risk in the manager's own deals (Delaware Life: $1.4bn → $17bn, 39%).
  13. A sponsor pays a direct lender 150–250bp more than syndicated debt and accepts quarterly maintenance covenants. What is it buying? Certainty and speed: no rating process, no syndication flex, one committed price that can pre-empt an auction, and a small lender group that can approve add-on money or an amendment in days. The covenants are the price of that relationship.
  14. An IG dealer quotes a bond at 118/115. Which side is the bid, and why does the HY desk quote 99/99.5 instead? 118 is the bid: a higher spread means a lower price, which is where a dealer buys. HY and distressed trade on dollar price because credit risk, not rates, drives the value, and huge spreads are meaningless as quotes.
  15. In Gatto's uptier, the minority's loan falls from 85 to 30 though the company's cash flows haven't changed. What changed, and what document feature allowed it? Its rank: $1.2bn of new debt now sits ahead of it. A simple-majority amendment right let the majority permit senior debt and then use the new money to retire its own old loans.
  16. You bought unsecured bonds at 40, the company later sells for $800M against $700M of debt, and you got zero. How? A judge valued it at $400M in bankruptcy, below the $500M secured claim, so secured lenders took all the new equity. Being right on value isn't enough; the valuation ruling decides.
  17. Why can an interval fund suffer worse fire sales in a rush than a non-traded BDC? It is legally required to make periodic repurchase offers, so it must keep paying out, while a non-traded BDC can suspend redemptions or convert to a drawdown fund and sell assets on its own schedule.
  18. A fund announces redemption requests equal to 30% of NAV with a 7% cap. Why might real demand for cash be lower, and why might the better funds see the most requests? Investors over-request, since pro-rated payouts are a share of what they ask for. And in a scramble people pull from funds still paying at or above NAV (Kroboth's cash machine), not the worst ones.
  19. Kroboth lends $30M against a law firm's case book the firm values at $800M. What is he actually underwriting? Not the cases (diversification handles that) but the firm as a business: will it overspend and run out of money before cases pay, and is he first money out with a fixed maturity?
